name: The Bielefeld Conspiracy
title: A Million Euros to Prove a City Is Fake
claims: Bielefeld conspiracy is a satirical theory that Bielefeld, Germany, does not exist | 1
Bielefeld population 341,755 as of December 2021; more than 340,000; Germany's 18th largest city | 1, 2
The theory says an entity called SIE ("they") conspired with authorities to create the illusion of the city | 1
The theory rests on three questions (know anyone from Bielefeld, been to Bielefeld, know anyone who has) | 1
A majority are expected to answer no; anyone answering yes is dismissed as in on it or deceived | 1
Origins and reasons are not part of the original theory | 1
Speculated originators jokingly include the CIA, Mossad, or aliens using Bielefeld University as a spaceship disguise | 1, 2
First posted on German Usenet newsgroup de.talk.bizarre on 16 May 1994 | 1
Newsweek dates the start to 1993 | 2
At a 1993 party a friend of the poster met someone from Bielefeld and said "Das gibt's doch gar nicht" (Wikipedia version) | 1
Newsweek says the poster himself said the phrase to the man from Bielefeld | 2
Phrase means "Unbelievable!" and "That doesn't exist"; the second meaning spread online | 1
Newsweek renders it colloquially as "there's nothing there" but literally "that doesn't exist" | 2
In a TV interview for the 10th anniversary, the poster said the myth originated from his posting, intended only as a joke | 1
The idea formed at a party talking to an avid reader of New Age magazines, and from a car journey past Bielefeld when the Autobahn exit was closed | 1
A historian said "'Bielefeld' defines nondescript"; the city has no major institutions or tourist attractions and is not on a major river | 1
Newsweek describes the city as having no major landmarks or geographical features | 2
The post became an early meme; by 1999 it was a topic of national conversation | 2
On April Fools' Day 1999 the city council released the press statement "Bielefeld gibt es doch!" | 1, 2
City sought to build a national image; ten years on, the mayor's office still received calls and e-mails doubting the city's existence | 1
In November 2012 Chancellor Angela Merkel referred to the conspiracy, speaking of a town hall meeting in Bielefeld: "if it exists at all", "I had the impression that I was there" | 1
Newsweek quotes Merkel as saying "...if it even exists" in a 2012 speech | 2
The 800th anniversary in 2014 used the motto "Das gibt's doch gar nicht" | 1
Mayor Pit Clausen called "Bielefeld doesn't exist" a great opener for conversation and said they'd have to come up with one otherwise (via CityMetric, per Newsweek) | 2
In August 2019 the council offered €1 million for "incontrovertible evidence" of nonexistence, to increase interest in the city | 1
Newsweek reported the offer as about $1.1 million | 2
No one proved non-existence, so the city considers the conspiracy ended | 1
The city erected a glacial erratic block near the Leineweber monument in the historic center with a QR code linking to background information | 1
In 2009 film students at Bielefeld University started a feature film project, financed by the university and local sponsors, mostly students and employees, with a few professionals | 1
The film premiered in Bielefeld on 2 June 2010 | 1
Books include "Rätselhaftes Bielefeld. Die Verschwörung" (2010), a novel of the film (2010), and "Gibt es Bielefeld oder gibt es Bielefeld nicht?" (2013) | 1

List of similar satirical conspiracy theories about other places (Australia, Dingwall, Acre, Finland, Leiria, Petah Tikva, Ness Tziona, Molise, Wyoming, La Pampa, Paraguay, Tlaxcala, Drenthe, Kilkis, Semnan, Saitama, Zhytomyr, Hasselt, Murcia, Teruel, Rancagua, Barrancabermeja, Leitrim, Russia outside the Moscow Ring Road) | 1
BBC World Service and The New York Times referenced the conspiracy in 2025 when Arminia Bielefeld surprisingly became a DFB-Pokal finalist | 1

sources.title: A Germany City is Offering $1.1 Million to Prove it Doesn’t Exist - Newsweek
